In the early spring of 1844, a little-remembered German clockmaker named Johann Escher sketched a curious device in his workshop journal. It was never built, yet the drawing still survives in the archives of the Museum für Technik in Dresden: a pocket watch whose hands revolve counterclockwise while a second, hidden dial inside the case records the owner’s memories in neatly inscribed, microscopic script. Escher claimed the watch would “wind backward through recollection even as the world goes forward,” creating a portable paradox—an object that moves in two temporal directions at once. Scholars dismiss the watch as a fanciful doodle, but I have always felt the notion reveals something essential about how human beings inhabit time. Our lives unwind forward in pulses of cause and effect, yet we perpetually rewind ourselves through memory, story, and imagination. We are, in effect, living Escher-watches: devices that carry the present into the future by steadily ticking, even as a hidden mechanism reverses direction, transcribing what has just slipped away.

I have been thinking about that image ever since I first saw the drawing reproduced in a footnote of a book on obsolete inventions. The problem of time—its passing, its accumulation, its apparently nonnegotiable arrow—haunts anyone who attempts to describe experience. Words themselves are minute gears in a watch not unlike Escher’s: every sentence nudges the reader forward, yet each noun or verb also points backward to what it evokes, what once was, or what might have been. Writing is time travel by grammar. A writer collapses an event spread over days or centuries into the span of a paragraph. Meanwhile, a reader unfolds that same paragraph inside the space of an afternoon. The result is an asynchrony so common we stop noticing its wonder. And still, inside the alchemy, a question persists: how do we hold on to the moments that matter?

Consider the way smell triggers recollection. My grandmother kept lemon verbena on a kitchen windowsill. Whenever I brush the leaves of the same plant in my own apartment, thirty-five years vanish: I am six again, balanced on a stool, watching her stir batter for a cake that will be eaten by relatives long gone. There is no rational path that carries me from my modern sink to that vanished room in under a heartbeat, but a volatile molecule travels through my nose and detonates a neural constellation. Scientists can map the circuit; poets try to name the longing. Neither quite suffices. The mechanism remains as improbable as Escher’s watch: two movements, forward and back, overlapping in a single, impossible instant.

If personal memory works like a hidden dial, collective memory works like a public clock tower. The face is visible to everyone, its bell tolls at regular intervals, and its scale governs daily existence. We set school schedules, work shifts, and train timetables by shared agreement on the hour. Yet collective clocks are susceptible to selective amnesia. Entire histories are left unwound, stored in locked attics or misfiled archives. When a marginalized community insists, “Remember us,” they are winding the collective mechanism in reverse, retrieving hours that official narrative allowed to run down. When public monuments are removed or renamed, the apparent forward march of dates halts and reverses briefly: citizens argue about which fragments of the unwound tape deserve to be placed back on the spool. The politics of memory is a politics of timekeeping.

Some philosophers argue that time is an illusion, a convenience of perception layered over a more fundamental, atemporal reality. Others claim the arrow of time is as real as gravity. I am no physicist, but I find myself sympathetic to both camps. On a purely human level, time is both the most concrete and the most vaporous substance we know. You can set a metronome to mark seconds with unwavering precision, and you can simultaneously feel an hour elongate to the point of breaking when you wait for difficult news. The relativity of lived time is not the relativity of Einstein’s equations, but it may be equally dramatic for the soul.

One afternoon I watched a swarm of mayflies hatch over a lake. Their adult lifespan is less than a day. In that span, they must mate, lay eggs, avoid the swipes of feeding fish, and die. To them, a sunrise is half a lifetime, a gust of wind a natural disaster. The idea forced me to recalibrate my sense of urgency. If I had only twenty hours in which to accomplish everything that constituted success in my species, how frantic would I be? How attuned to every flicker of danger, every nuance of opportunity? And if, conversely, I lived as long as a redwood—thousands of years—would I feel the ticking of motivation at all, or drift in a serenity too slow for my current biology to imagine? Escher’s watch sits in my pocket either way, recording the micro-events of a day or the macro-rings of a millennium, but the speed at which its visible hands sweep the dial changes with perspective.

There is a second sketch beside the first in Escher’s notebook. It shows a watchcase half-buried in soil, sprouting roots, a tiny tree emerging where the winder should be. Perhaps he understood that even metal succumbs to the rhythms of growth and decay, that chronology and ecology speak the same dialect. A fallen log becomes nurse to seedlings; a discarded gadget becomes archaeological evidence. One era’s refuse is another era’s reliquary. The hidden dial inside such an object continues to inscribe stories long after the owner is gone. Future hands may retrieve the device, polish its corroded face, and ask: who wound this, and what moments did it capture?

Lately I find solace in small rituals that bend time’s apparent sovereignty. I cook meals that take four hours of simmering; the pot steadies my pulse to a medieval slowness. I handwrite letters on paper because an envelope’s journey through postal corridors adds delicious anticipation that no instantaneous email can match. I read nineteenth-century novels whose descriptive passages unspool at a gait considered extravagant by contemporary markets. These practices are not retro affectations so much as exercises in temporal plurality: reminders that the single standardized tempo of high-speed life is a cultural choice, not an ontological rule. By voluntarily slowing down, I persuade the inner dial to carve deeper grooves rather than madly skipping across the record.

Does all this mean we should revere the past at the expense of the future? Not at all. The counterclockwise motion of Escher’s hidden dial is only half the mechanism, and a watch that runs backward alone is useless for catching a train. My grandfather fought in a war that nearly erased his generation, but he refused to dwell in trauma. Instead, he built radios from surplus parts and spent weekends teaching neighborhood children how to align coils, solder joints, and chase distant signals bouncing off the ionosphere. He knew understanding the past is preparation, not imprisonment. The energy released by remembering can, paradoxically, propel us forward—so long as we keep one eye on the other set of hands sweeping relentlessly clockwise.

Near the exit of the Dresden museum, a modern installation invites visitors to write a single memory on a strip of archival paper and feed it into a glass column. A slow spiral of air keeps the fragments suspended in perpetual drift. Each evening the curators shut off the fan for fifteen seconds, letting the memories settle randomly before they re-activate the updraft. It is an elegant rebuttal to linear narrative: at any moment, a scrap from 2012 brushes against another from 1897 or 2025, and for those heartbeats they occupy the same altitude. The piece reminds me that chronology is only one choreography among many. Memories bump into possibilities; forgotten tragedies kiss newborn hopes; your grandmother’s lemon verbena collides with my mayfly swarm. A spectator watching the column sees neither past nor future in isolation, but a storm of now-moments twirling in luminous flux.

When I step away from that column—imaginary or real—I feel the downward tug of everyday obligations: deadlines, appointments, the beeps of devices. Yet somewhere just under the skin, the secret dial keeps etching a pale script: coffee shared with a friend, leaf shadows on a sidewalk, an overheard phrase in a bus queue that might become the seed of a story. These threads are fragile, yet together they weave the only durable fabric we possess. We are both the loom and the tapestry, both the clock face and the concealed recorder. Time claims us, but we annotate its claim with memory, with narrative, with love. And if one day an archaeologist unearths the pocket watch of my life, I hope they find the hidden inscription still legible: Here lived someone who listened, someone who wound the springs of attention both forward and back, until the clatter of passing seconds sounded, at last, like music.
